RESOURCES_01: I realized there’s not a lot of resources to help neurodivergent grad student mentors… we usually struggle with balancing our different obligations and also communicating requirements and expectations and we feel the need to fill in the gap of our stakeholders expectations. Also, I would have loved resources on how to manage stakeholders expectations: this project is designated to mentor undergrads on research practices, and not as a side project a PhD candidate takes on to produce data. So, productivity is at a lower threshold naturally.
MENTOR_FORMAT_2: I love the idea of discovery hubs as a department-agnostic research mentorship structure. I feel it works best for projects that are more individual-ish, like the humanities and social sciences. For the natural science fields, for example, a lot of the research happens in groups: shared equipment, lab meetings, joint experiments. And as such, not having a centralized department or lab that’s sponsoring this makes it really hard to mentor undergrads since there’s a very loose institutional home for lab work.
OPPORTUNITIES:
I think it should be offered to students who want it, not to all grad students. Some students see a PhD as a means to an end, as opposed to an opportunity to pursue scholarship that’s exciting, and contribute to the development of the next generation of scientists and thinkers. 

Though, for anyone who wants to go into academia, I think they must have at least one experience mentoring undergrads just because many people who become PIs don’t really know how to mentor, and that’s something that’s not tested greatly during faculty interviews. I think a lot of the faculty interviews focus on the person’s accomplishments as a scientist, and not on their teaching or mentorship philosophy too.

RESOURCES_01: Training materials were decent but I would have really appreciated a more application-focused approach to improving mentorship with active guidance on how I can assess my effectiveness as a mentor and address my shortcomings.
MENTOR_FORMAT_2: The Discovery Hub provides a framework and accountability for ensuring undergraduates consistently work towards a research goal, while supporting me with resources and guidance to facilitate my mentees development. The recruitment process was extremely productive and frictionless, expediting the opportunities I received to find promising undergraduates who are interested in pursuing research. The Discovery Hub's emphasis on a deliverable is also wonderful, as it gives mentees something tangible to strive towards throughout the research experience and helps keep them motivated. I think more emphasis should be placed on making monthly events mandatory for the mentees. My biggest difficulty working within the confines of the Discovery Hub was change to program communication from email to bCourses. I repeatedly found assignments locked or past due whenever I checked in bCourses, and greatly preferred email communication as an easily accessible way to respond to all reflections and forms. This was particularly frustrating as the assignments were deeply beneficial to my self development.
OPPORTUNITIES: Yes, I found that delegating tasks and planning research timelines for mentees helped develop my own awareness of the long-term goals of my project in a concrete manner. The ability to sustain multiple lines of inquiry simultaneously through delegation and technical support is an essential skill. As a researcher with high technical proficiency in my field, acting in a directing role stimulated my growth beyond performing my own experiments.
TESTIM_01: Working in single-molecule research is extremely demanding on your time and attention. The Discovery Hub was my first experience working with undergraduates. I now have a realistic understanding of what is accomplishable for an undergraduate in my field of research. This understanding greatly changed how I view project development in three ways. First, I am more critical about the research question being answered by a proposed experiment. As a graduate student, it is answer to consider an alternative or tangential question within one week of work, but undergraduates do not have such time. Secondly, I now plan training and mentee involvement in a project by determining the fastest way for them to learn data collection and analysis in order to fuel critical hypothesis-driven thinking (instead of the other way around).Third, I am better equipped to assess the feasibility of n undergraduate project during the school year. Instead of answering an entire question, it is much better to completely characterize one condition, understand the scientific impetus, and be able to communicate the intellectual implications of the results.
TESTIM_03: The Discovery Research Hub has truly opened my eyes to the clarity needed when to train and manage researchers in a productive fashion. I am beginning to understand the complexity and skills necessary to develop a research project, not simply to accomplish individual experiments. The process is thrilling and satisfying and has made me excited to purse academic careers in the near future.

INTEREST_06: I found that my undergraduates were not fluent in explaining our research to others, despite having spent a year in my research cluster and even attending a specialized conference. One workshop future Discovery Hub participants would benefit from is for undergraduates specifically: have them talk with their peers in the program about their research! We had such a workshop for the mentors in the Spring, and I believe the undergraduates would benefit even more from doing so. I would encourage making that workshop mandatory for undergraduates and doing it once each semester, the first time to learn how to introduce their research and the second time to learn how to share results/finding/next steps.

OPPORTUNITIES: Yes -- especially in the humanities, where "research" is less often carried out collaboratively, and there is almost no way to gain meaningful experience with the sorts of formal mentorship relationships involved in honors thesis advising or capstone projects. Teaching sections and composition courses alone doesn't prepare a doctoral student in the humanities for this sort of advising, which seriously hampers ABDs competing with more experienced candidates for jobs that require this kind of service on day one! The opportunity to work with advanced students within one's major or related majors feels like an indispensable complement to the pedagogical skills one develops when, e.g., teaching non-majors in a comp course. We all have some experience of trying to win over students who are disinclined or indifferent, but it's been lovely to be asked the kinds of questions that can only be asked by students who are *already* invested.

INTEREST_06:
Having completed two semesters with Berkeley Connect -- the departmental maximum -- the Discovery program would be my only means of participating in undergraduate mentorship during my final year as a doctoral student in the humanities at Cal. This program gave me the chance to continue working with undergraduate students whom I had already mentored more casually through Connect or taught in courses; the pedagogical relationships we were able to build within this framework have undoubtedly been the most rewarding of any I've built as a mentor and instructor.

As a mentor with Berkeley Connect this past fall, working mostly with students who recently transferred from community colleges across CA, many of my mentees were eager for insights into the research process and as much hands-on experience as they could get during their remaining two years at Cal. I drew on my experience with the Discovery program to help them plan thesis proposals, find relevant research opportunities, and explore options for postgrad research. I've kept in touch with many of these students, and would be grateful for the opportunity to work with them in some more formal capacity -- giving them the chance to earn course credit, or financial compensation if LAEP funding permits, while helping them become the scholars that they want to be on this shortened timeline.

For a doctoral candidate in my position, who still has not reached the quota of teaching semesters but faces a dearth of teaching appointments in my own department, continued participation in the Discovery program would help me develop further as a mentor and teacher. I would also be grateful for the chance to put my experience as a mentor, through Discovery as well as Connect, at the disposal of other graduate student mentors in turn -- something I was able to do last fall as the only member of our department's Berkeley Connect team to have served as a mentor the previous year, sharing  materials  and  practical insights with my fellow mentors and the incoming faculty director. If my service as a Pedagogy Mentor to other graduate instructors within my home department has taught me anything, it's that this kind of dialogue is indispensable in refining one's own thinking, enabling one to revisit the most fundamental premises of scholarly and pedagogical practice from new perspectives.
